# Going With the Stream—or Against It

*AN 4.5, the Anusota Sutta — set 2, The Basic Diagnosis and the Path*

<p class="reading-meta"><strong>Reading time:</strong> about 3 min · 416 words</p>

[Skip to the translation](#translation){ .reader-skip-link }

## Before you read

This teaching turns the path into one river image. Drifting downstream means
following the easy pull of sensual indulgence and harmful behavior. Going
upstream means resisting that pull, even when doing so feels difficult.

The first two descriptions are directions of movement, not permanent kinds
of human being. The last two use the early Buddhist map of awakening: one
person will not return to ordinary sensual existence, while the other has
completed the crossing. You can follow the practical image—drifting,
struggling, becoming steady, and reaching dry land—before deciding what you
think about the text's claims concerning rebirth.

One phrase is especially honest: a person may go upstream while distressed
and in tears. Beginning to act against a well-established habit is not always
peaceful, but it changes the direction of travel.

## Translation

### Four Ways of Meeting the Stream

"Bhikkhus, four kinds of people are found in the world.

Which four?

A person going with the stream.

A person going against the stream.

A person standing firm.

And a brahmin who has crossed over, gone to the far shore, and stands on dry
land.

### Going With the Stream

Who is the person who goes with the stream?

It is someone who indulges in sensual pleasures and does harmful actions.

This is called a person who goes with the stream.

### Going Against the Stream

Who is the person who goes against the stream?

It is someone who does not indulge in sensual pleasures or do harmful
actions. Even while suffering and distressed—weeping, with tears on their
face—they live the full and pure spiritual life.

This is called a person who goes against the stream.

### Standing Firm

Who is the person who stands firm?

It is someone who, with the wearing away of the five lower fetters, is
spontaneously reborn elsewhere. They reach final nibbāna there and will not
return from that world.

This is called a person who stands firm.

### Reaching Dry Land

Who is the brahmin who has crossed over, gone to the far shore, and stands on
dry land?

It is someone who, with the wearing away of the outflows, realizes for
themselves the release of mind and release through discernment, both free of
outflows. They enter and live in these releases here and now.

This is called a brahmin who has crossed over, gone to the far shore, and
stands on dry land.

These are the four kinds of people found in the world.

### The Four in Verse

People unrestrained in sensual pleasures,
still caught in passion and enjoying those pleasures here,
return to birth and old age again and again.
Overwhelmed by ignorant wanting, they go with the stream.

So a clear-sighted person, with remembering established,
does not indulge in sensual pleasures or harmful actions.
Even through pain, they should let sensual pleasures go.
Such a person is said to go against the stream.

Someone who has abandoned five stains,
a fully developed trainee who cannot fall back,
master of their heart, with their faculties composed,
is called a person who stands firm.

Whoever has fully understood things high and low
has swept them away; they have ended and are no more.
That sage has completed the spiritual life,
gone to the world's end, and reached the far shore."

The fifth discourse is finished.

<dt><dfn>against the stream</dfn></dt>
<dd>Resisting the current of sensual indulgence and harmful action, even when changing direction is difficult.</dd>
<dt><dfn>bhikkhus</dfn></dt>
<dd>Buddhist monks -- those who have left household life to practise full time. The Buddha&#x27;s usual way of addressing the assembly, roughly &quot;friends&quot; in force.</dd>
<dt><dfn>birth</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;jāti&quot; -- being born, and the link that ageing and dying depend on in the dependent-arising sequence. In MN 141 the word appears once in its everyday sense instead, in a simile about a mother.</dd>
<dt><dfn>brahmin</dfn></dt>
<dd>Originally a member of ancient India&#x27;s hereditary priestly class. These texts sometimes reuse the title for an ideal practitioner who has completed the path, so context determines whether caste or conduct is meant.</dd>
<dt><dfn>crossed over</dfn></dt>
<dd>Having completed the crossing rather than merely moving toward the other side. This preserves the river image used for completion of the path.</dd>
<dt><dfn>faculties</dfn></dt>
<dd>The capacities used in practice—especially confidence, energy, remembering, composure, and discernment—considered as abilities that can be trained and brought into balance.</dd>
<dt><dfn>far shore</dfn></dt>
<dd>The safe side of the river image: the completion reached after crossing beyond the forces that keep a person bound.</dd>
<dt><dfn>final nibbāna</dfn></dt>
<dd>The final-completion use of nibbāna language. It is not a synonym for death, annihilation, or heaven.</dd>
<dt><dfn>five lower fetters</dfn></dt>
<dd>Five patterns said to bind a person to ordinary sensual existence: self-view, doubt, grasping at rules and observances, sensual passion, and aversion.</dd>
<dt><dfn>heart</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;citta&quot; -- the affective or feeling side of mind: the part that takes on a mood, wants, leans, reacts, and can be gladdened, steadied, trained, and released. It is sometimes called the &quot;heart-mind&quot; or &quot;feeling mind&quot;; here &quot;heart&quot; does not mean merely emotion or the physical organ.</dd>
<dt><dfn>ignorant wanting</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;taṇhā&quot; (often translated &quot;craving&quot;), chosen to keep visible that the wanting in question is driven by not seeing clearly, not just ordinary desire.</dd>
<dt><dfn>outflows</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;āsavā&quot; -- deep-running habits that keep seeping out and driving behaviour, classically sensuality, becoming, and ignorance. Often translated &quot;taints&quot; or &quot;defilements.&quot;</dd>
<dt><dfn>release of mind</dfn></dt>
<dd>Release described from the mind or heart side of experience, often paired with release through discernment.</dd>
<dt><dfn>release through discernment</dfn></dt>
<dd>Release described from the clear-understanding side, paired with release of mind rather than reduced to intellectual knowledge.</dd>
<dt><dfn>remembering</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;sati&quot; -- actively keeping what matters in mind and returning to it when it is lost, not bare attention to whatever happens to be present.</dd>
<dt><dfn>sensual pleasures</dfn></dt>
<dd>Enjoyable sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches when they are being pursued and consumed as sources of satisfaction.</dd>
<dt><dfn>spiritual life</dfn></dt>
<dd>The Buddhist path of practice as a whole -- not just a set of beliefs, but a whole way of living.</dd>
<dt><dfn>spontaneously reborn</dfn></dt>
<dd>Reborn fully formed rather than through a womb, egg, or moisture. AN 4.5 uses this traditional cosmological description for a non-returner.</dd>
<dt><dfn>stands firm</dfn></dt>
<dd>AN 4.5&#x27;s river image for a non-returner: someone no longer being swept back into ordinary sensual existence, though the crossing is not yet complete.</dd>
<dt><dfn>trainee</dfn></dt>
<dd>Someone who has entered the noble path and is still completing the training; not a beginner.</dd>
<dt><dfn>wearing away</dfn></dt>
<dd>The gradual using-up of something until it is exhausted and finished -- used especially of what has to run out before there is release.</dd>
<dt><dfn>with the stream</dfn></dt>
<dd>Following the easy current of sensual indulgence and harmful action. In AN 4.5 this is a warning, not praise for being flexible.</dd>
<dt><dfn>world</dfn></dt>
<dd>A word whose scope shifts with the teaching. It can mean the lived world built through the senses and the mind, or the wider physical cosmos. The surrounding passage shows which sense is meant.</dd>
<dt><dfn>world&#x27;s end</dfn></dt>
<dd>In AN 4.5, the end of the experienced world as a field of bondage -- not a geographic edge of the earth.</dd>
